paragraphs.text: ON PERFECTION, AND WHAT KIND OF PERSON THE CHRISTIAN OUGHT TO BE: TO OLYMPIUS THE MONK. Your eagerness to learn how one might be made perfect through a life of virtue, so that your life may be blameless in every respect, befits the way of life you have chosen. For my part, I would have counted it of the highest importance that examples of what you are striving for could be found in my own life, so that I might give you the instruction you seek through deeds before words. For then the guidance toward what is good would be trustworthy, since the life would be in harmony with the words. I pray that this may one day come about; but since I do not yet see myself as someone who can display a life in place of a discourse, and so that I may not seem altogether useless to you and of no help toward your goal, I have decided to set out for you the things toward which the exact life must strive, and I begin my discourse here. Our good Master Jesus Christ has graciously given us a share in his adored name, so that we are named from nothing else that belongs to us. Whether someone happens to be rich and nobly born, or low-born and poor, or is known for some occupation or office, all such names are set aside, and he has bestowed one sovereign title on those who have believed in him: to be called Christians. Since this grace has been confirmed to us from above, we must first understand the greatness of the gift, so as to give worthy thanks to the God who has bestowed such great things; and then we must show ourselves through our life to be such as the power of this great name demands. Now the greatness of the gift we have been counted worthy of, by being named together with the Master of our life, would become clear to us if we came to know the very meaning of the name of Christ, so as to understand, when by this word we call upon the Lord of all in our prayers, what notion we take up in our souls, or what it is we have in mind through this name

when we believe that we are calling upon him reverently. Once we have understood this, we will then learn clearly, as a consequence, what kind of people we ought to show ourselves to be through our earnestness in how we live, using the name as our teacher and guide for life. If, then, we take holy Paul as our leader in these two matters, we will have the surest guidance toward clarity about what we are seeking. For he, more precisely than anyone, understood what Christ is, and showed by what he did what kind of person the one named after him ought to be. He imitated him so vividly that he displayed his own Master formed in himself: through the most exact imitation, the form of his soul was changed into that of the prototype, so that it no longer seemed to be Paul who lived and spoke, but Christ himself living in him. As this noble man says, aware of his own goods: "Since you are seeking proof of the Christ who speaks in me," and, "It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me." This man, then, made known to us the meaning of the name of Christ, saying that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. He also called him peace, and light unapproachable in which God dwells; sanctification and redemption; great high priest, and Passover; propitiation of souls; radiance of glory and imprint of substance, and maker of the ages; spiritual food and drink, rock and water; foundation of faith and head of the corner; image of the invisible God, and great God; head of the body of the Church; firstborn of the new creation; firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep; firstborn from the dead; firstborn among many brothers; mediator between God and human beings; only-begotten Son crowned with glory and honor; Lord of glory; and the beginning of all that exists (for he says of him, "who is the beginning"); and besides these, king of righteousness, king of peace, and king of all, holding the power of a kingship that has no bounds. And there are many other such titles, too many to count easily. All of these, taken together, since the meaning of each title contributes its own share toward displaying what is signified, give us some impression of the meaning of the name of Christ, showing us as much of his ineffable majesty as our souls are able to grasp. Now the dignity of kingship surpasses every dignity, authority, and dominion; and the title "Christ" properly and primarily signifies royal power (for anointing, as we have learned from the histories, came before kingship); and kingship includes all the power of the other titles. Therefore whoever has understood the things it includes has also understood the power that includes all the particulars. And this is the kingship of which the name "Christ" is the indicating title. Since, then,

our good Master has given us a share in the greatest, most divine, and first of names, so that those honored with the title of Christ are called Christians, it would be necessary that all the names that interpret this word should be seen in us as well, so that the title may not be a false name for us but may have the testimony of our life. For a thing does not come to be by being called something. Rather, the underlying nature, whatever it happens to be, is made known through the meaning of the name that properly belongs to it. I mean something like this: if someone gave a tree or a rock the name "human being," would the plant or the stone become a human being because of the name? Certainly not. It must first be a human being, and only then be called by the name of its nature. For not even in the case of likenesses do names carry their proper sense, as when someone calls a statue a man, or a representation a horse. If anything is to be named properly and truthfully, its nature will in every case show that the name is true. The material that has received the likeness is called whatever it actually is, bronze or stone or something else of the kind, on which art has imposed the form, shaping it as it saw fit. So those who name themselves after Christ must first become what the name means, and only then apply the title to themselves. And just as someone who wished to distinguish the real human being from the one called by the same name in an image would make the distinction from their distinctive properties (calling the one a rational, thinking living being, and the other lifeless matter that has taken on the form through imitation), so too we will recognize the Christian, both the one who truly is one and the one who only seems to be, through the properties that appear in their features. And the marks of the true Christian are all those things we have understood concerning Christ. Those we are able to imitate, we imitate; those our nature cannot attain to by imitation, we revere and worship. Therefore all the names that interpret the meaning of Christ must shine in the Christian's life, some through imitation and others through worship, if the man of God is to be complete, as the Apostle says, never mutilating his completeness through vice. For think of those who fashion mythical monsters, whether in words or by the art of painting: bull-headed creatures, horse-centaurs, serpent-footed beings, or some other such thing put together from different kinds. They do not direct their imitation toward nature's archetype; rather, showing [?] nature through this absurd invention, they fashion something else, not a human being, shaping it toward

[?] showing the body of his conduct out of keeping with his faith; or growing into one with the fury of serpents and turning savage in the likeness of these reptiles; or joining the horse's frenzied lust to human form, and becoming a kind of double-natured centaur made of the rational and the irrational. One can see many such people. Some lead a decent life with a calf's head, that is, in the doctrine of idolatry (as they paint the Minotaur). Others, with a Christian face, fit a beastly body to their life, like the centaurs or serpent-footed creatures they fashion. So, if the Christian is to be recognized as a human being is recognized by a human body, the believer must bear stamped on his life the marks of all the goods we understand concerning Christ. For to be in some respects what the name requires, while in others leaning toward the opposite, is nothing other than to cut oneself in two and become one's own enemy, at war within oneself through virtue and vice, irreconcilable with oneself and inconsistent in one's life. "For what fellowship has light with darkness?" says the Apostle. Since the opposition to light cannot be mixed with it and admits no go-between, the one who holds on to both and lets go of neither is necessarily torn apart himself by the opposition of things that stand against each other. He becomes light and darkness at once in a mixed life: faith pours in its illumination, while the dark life blackens the brightness that comes from the word. Since, then, there can be no mixing and no agreement between light and darkness, the one who embraces both opposites becomes his own enemy, split in two between virtue and vice, and drawn up in battle against himself. Now, just as with two enemies it is impossible for both to be victors over each other (for the victory of one certainly brings about the death of the opponent), so too in this civil war, which arises from a mixed life, the better side cannot possibly win unless the other is utterly destroyed. For how will the army of godliness prevail over vice while the wicked phalanx of the enemy still stands against it? If the better is to win, the opposing side must certainly be slain. And thus virtue will win the victory over vice when everything hostile to it, with the help of our reasoning as an ally, has retreated into non-existence. Then is fulfilled what was said through prophecy in the person of God: "I will kill, and I will make alive." For the good in me cannot live in any other way than by being brought to life through the death of the enemy. But as long as we cling to both, grasping each of the opposites with one hand, it is impossible to share in both at the same time.

For when someone has seized hold of vice, virtue has slipped from his grasp. Let us then return to the argument we began with: that there is one road for lovers of virtue to the pure and divine life, namely to know what the name of Christ signifies, to which our life too must be conformed, shaped toward virtue by the impression made by the other names. So, all the words and names interpreting the meaning of Christ that we gathered at the beginning of this discourse from the holy voice of Paul, we will set before us for the task at hand and make them our surest guide to the life of virtue, imitating some, as was said earlier, and worshiping and revering others. Let us follow the order in which they were listed. We will begin, then, with the first: "Christ," he says, "is the power of God and the wisdom of God." Through these words we first learn, from the title of Christ, the notions befitting God, through which the name becomes worthy of reverence to us. For the whole creation, both what is known by the senses and what lies beyond the grasp of the senses, came into being through him and holds together in him. So, in defining the presence [?] of Christ, the maker of all things, wisdom is necessarily joined with power. We understand this through the pairing of these two words, power and wisdom: these great and ineffable wonders of creation would not exist unless wisdom had conceived their coming into being, and power had accompanied wisdom to complete what was conceived, so that conceptions become works. Fittingly, then, the meaning of Christ is divided into a twofold impression, wisdom and power. When we look at the greatness of the structure of all that exists, we come to understand his ineffable power through what we perceive. When we consider that things which did not exist came into being, the manifold nature of existing things having been given substance by a divine nod, then we are to believe that Christ is incomprehensible wisdom. For whatever someone calls upon in prayer and looks toward with the eye of the soul, he draws to himself through prayer. And so the one who looks toward power (and Christ is the power) is strengthened with power in the inner man, as the Apostle says; and the one who [looks to] wisdom [?] becomes wise, as Proverbs says. Therefore the one who is named together with Christ, who is both power and wisdom, is also named together with power, being made strong against sin, and he will show wisdom in himself by choosing what is better. When wisdom and power are displayed in us, wisdom choosing the good and power carrying out what was conceived, the perfection of life is achieved through both woven together. So too, having understood Christ as peace, we will show that the title of Christ is true of us if we show Christ in our life through the peace within us. He put the hostility to death,

as the Apostle says. So let us not bring it back to life within ourselves, but show it to be dead in our life. Let us never, through anger and holding grudges, raise up against ourselves, to the ruin of our souls, what God rightly put to death for our salvation, bringing about an evil resurrection of what had died well. Rather, if we have Christ, who is peace, let us too put hostility to death within ourselves, so that what we believe of him we may also achieve in our own life. For just as he broke down the dividing wall that separated us and created in himself one new man out of the two, making peace, so let us too bring to reconciliation not only those who fight against us from outside but also those who rebel within us, so that the flesh may no longer desire against the spirit, nor the spirit against the flesh. Instead, with the mind of the flesh made subject to the divine law, let us be at peace within ourselves, refashioned into the one new and peaceful man, the two having become one. For the definition of peace is the harmony of things that were at odds. So when the civil war is removed from our nature, then we too, at peace within ourselves, become peace, showing the title of Christ to be true and proper in us. And understanding Christ as the true light, which falsehood cannot approach, we learn this: that our life too must be illumined by the rays of the true Father. The rays of the Sun of righteousness are the virtues, which stream forth to illumine us. Through them we come to put off the works of darkness and to walk decently as in the day; and, renouncing the hidden things of shame and doing everything in the light, we become light ourselves, so as to shine for others too through our works, which is the property of light. And if we understand Christ to be sanctification, [?] from every profane and impure act and thought, confessing the power of sanctification not in word but

Having learned that Christ is redemption, he who gave himself as a ransom for us, we are taught this by such a word: that, giving us immortality as a price, as it were, for each soul, he made those he bought back from death by means of life his own possession. If, then, we have become slaves of the one who redeemed us, we will certainly look to our Master, so as no longer to live for ourselves but for the one who acquired us with life as the price of exchange. For we are no longer our own masters; the one who bought us is Lord, and we are his possessions. Therefore the will of the one who is master will be the law of our life. For just as, when death ruled over us, the law of sin governed our conduct, so now, since we have become

the possession of life, our way of life must be brought into line with what now rules us, so that we never turn aside from the will of life and, through sin, desert once more to the wicked tyrant of our souls, I mean death. The same thought will bring us close to Christ, whether we hear from Paul that he is the Passover or that he is the high priest. For truly Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed for us; yet the priest who offers the sacrifice to God is no one other than Christ himself. "For he offered himself," it says, "as an offering and sacrifice for us." Through these words, then, we learn this: whoever looks to him who offered himself as an offering and sacrifice and became the Passover will also present himself to God as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing, becoming reasonable worship. And the manner of this sacred service is not to be conformed to this age, but to be transformed by the renewal of one's mind, so as to discern what the will of God is, what is good and pleasing and perfect. For while the flesh is still alive and has not been offered up according to the spiritual law, the good will of God cannot be displayed in it, because the mind of the flesh is hostile to God and does not submit to God's law; indeed it cannot, as long as the flesh lives. But once the flesh has been offered through the life-giving sacrifice, by putting to death the earthly members through which the passions operate, the pleasing and perfect will of God will be accomplished without hindrance in the life of those who have believed in him. So too, when Christ is understood as a propitiation in his own blood, he teaches whoever understands this that each person should become a propitiation for himself, purifying his soul by putting his members to death. And when Christ is called the radiance of glory and the imprint of substance, through these words we take in thoughts of his adored majesty. For Paul, truly inspired by God and taught by God, searched out the obscure and hidden things of the divine mysteries in the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God. He received illuminations from God for understanding things unsearchable and untraceable, but since his tongue was weaker than his mind, he indicated them through certain riddles, as far as the hearing of those who received his understanding of the mystery could contain it, uttering only as much as words were able to serve his thought. For although he had understood all that human capacity can contain, he presents the [account] of the transcendent essence as beyond reach and beyond the grasp of human reasoning.

So when he speaks of what is contemplated concerning it, such as peace, power, life, righteousness, light, truth, and the like, he declared that any account of that essence itself is wholly beyond grasp, saying that God has never been seen and never will be seen. "Whom no one," he says, "has seen, nor can see" [?]

[?] For this reason, as he sought a name for what reasoning cannot grasp and found none expressive enough to convey what lies beyond comprehension, he called that which transcends every good, which can be neither worthily conceived nor put into words, "glory" and "substance." The essence that transcends all beings he left unnamed. But to explain the Son's close union with the Father and his inseparability from him, and that he is contemplated together with the boundless and eternal Father in a boundless and eternal way, he calls him "the radiance of glory" and "the express image of substance." By "radiance" he shows that the Son shares the Father's nature, and by "image" that he is of equal standing. For nothing is conceived as standing between the radiance and the nature that sends it forth, nor is the image in any way less than the substance it expresses. Rather, whoever has conceived of the radiating nature has certainly perceived its radiance as well, and whoever has grasped in his mind the greatness of the substance certainly measures the substance by the image in which it appears. That is why he also calls the Lord "the form of God." He does not belittle the Lord by the notion of form. Rather, by means of the form he shows the greatness of the Son, in whom the majesty of the Father is contemplated, nowhere exceeding its own form and never found outside the image that belongs to it. For there is nothing in the Father that is formless or lacking in beauty, nothing that does not delight in the loveliness of the Only-begotten. That is why the Lord says, "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father," meaning by this that there is neither any deficiency nor any excess. Moreover, by saying that he upholds all things by the word of his power, he resolves the perplexity of those who busy themselves with what cannot be searched out. These people inquire into the account of matter and never set a limit to their curiosity. They say: How can matter come from what is immaterial? How can quantity come from what has no quantity, shape from the shapeless, color from the invisible, and what is bounded by its own measures from the unbounded? And if there is no quality in what is simple and uncompounded, where does matter come from, entangled as it is with the qualities that belong to it? All these questions and others like them are resolved by the one who said that the Word upholds all things by the word of his power, bringing them from non-being into existence. For all things that have received an immaterial nature have one cause of their existence: the word of the ineffable power. From this we are taught to look toward him from whom real beings take their origin. For if we were brought into being from there, and hold together in him, we must of necessity believe that nothing lies outside the knowledge of the one in whom we are, from whom we have come, and to whom we return. And with this way of thinking, it is reasonable to expect, a sinless life is achieved as well. For who, believing that he lives from him, through him and in him, would dare to make the one who holds each person's life within himself a witness of a life that is at odds with him? In calling the Lord spiritual food and drink, the divine

Apostle is suggesting that we understand from his words that human nature is not of a single kind but is a blend of the intelligible with the sensible, and that each of the elements we observe in ourselves has its own food: sensible food sustains the body, while spiritual nourishment produces in us the good health of the soul. In the body, the solid and liquid parts of food, mixed with other things, preserve our nature, being blended by the appropriate digestion with each of the elements of which we are compounded. In the same way and by analogy, Paul also divides intelligible food, calling one and the same thing both food and drink, as it is suitably adapted to the need of those who receive it. For to the weak and exhausted it becomes bread that strengthens the heart of man, while to those who are worn out by the hardships of this life, and so have grown thirsty, it becomes wine that brings the heart to gladness. By all this we should understand the power of the Word, by which the soul is nourished according to its need as it receives the grace that comes from him. This is what the prophet's figure means when he speaks of "a place of green pasture" and "water of rest" to signify the comfort the Word brings to the weary. But if someone, with the mystery in view, should say that the Lord is called food and drink in the proper sense, this too is not foreign to the proper meaning; for truly his flesh is food and truly his blood is drink. Under the first interpretation, however, participation in the Word is open to all who wish it: the Word becomes food and drink offered without distinction and received by those who seek him. Under the other sense, participation in such food and drink is not without examination and discernment, since the Apostle laid down: "Let each one examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment on himself." It seems to me that the evangelist had this in view when he carefully noted that at the time of the mystical Passion that noble councillor wrapped the Lord's body in a spotless, clean linen cloth and laid it in a new, clean tomb. In this way both the Apostle's command and the evangelist's observation become a law for all of us: to receive the holy body with a clean conscience, and if any stain of sin should be on us, to wash it away with the water of tears. Again, Christ is called a rock, and this name will benefit us by making us firm and immovable in a life of virtue, steadfast in enduring sufferings, and able to show a soul that resists and does not yield to any assault of sin. For through these and similar

things we too shall be rock, imitating in our changeable nature, as far as we can, the Master's unchangeable and immovable character. And if the wise master builder also calls him both the foundation of faith and the head of the corner, this too will prove useful to us in building a life of virtue. For these names teach us that the Lord is both the beginning and the end of every good way of life and of every good teaching and pursuit. For he is our hope, and Paul names him so. We understand the hope as the head, toward which every effort after virtue looks. And the beginning of this lofty tower-building of life is faith in him. On it, as on a foundation, we lay the beginnings of our life, and by daily good deeds we make pure thoughts and actions our law. In this way the head of the universe also becomes our head, fitting itself at the corner joint to the two walls of our life, the body and the soul, which are built up through decorum and purity. So if one of the two structures is missing, whether outward decorum is not built up together with purity of soul or the soul's virtue does not match what appears outwardly, Christ would not become the head of this half-finished life, since he fits himself only to the double structure that meets at the corner. For it is impossible to make a corner without two walls meeting. Our building will receive the beauty of the cornerstone only when the double life is laid out harmoniously on both sides along the straight rule of life by the line of the virtues, upright and undistorted, with nothing crooked or bent in it. Paul calls Christ the image of the invisible God, and also God over all and great God; for with these words too he proclaims the majesty of the true Master, saying, "of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ," and, "from whom is the Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever." By saying these things he teaches us that Christ is always what he is (and he is that which only He Who Is knows). As for human comprehension, however near to him progress may bring the one whose mind is set on things above, he always remains above by the same measure. This one, then, who is beyond all knowledge and comprehension, the inexpressible, unspeakable and indescribable, became the image of the invisible God out of love for humanity, in order to make you an image of God again. He did this so that in the very form he took on he might be formed in you, and that you in turn, through him, might be conformed to the stamp of the archetypal beauty and become what you were from the beginning. If, then, we too are to become the image of the invisible God, the form of our life ought to be shaped according to the pattern of life set before us. And what is this? That those who live in the flesh [1 Cor. 3[?]; Eph. 2:20[?]; Luke 20:17.]

should not live according to the flesh. For that archetypal image of the invisible God, who came to dwell among us through the Virgin, was tempted in every way in the likeness of human nature, but sin was the one thing he did not experience. "For he committed no sin," it says, "nor was deceit found in his mouth." Suppose we were being taught the art of painting, and the teacher set before us a beautifully painted figure on a panel. Each of us would have to imitate its beauty in his own painting, so that all our panels would be adorned after the model of beauty set before us. In the same way, each person is the painter of his own life. The artist of this work is free choice, and the colors for completing the image are the virtues [?]. So there is no small danger that we turn the imitation of the archetypal beauty into an ugly and misshapen mask, sketching with filthy colors the features of vice instead of the Master's form. Rather, as far as possible, we must take up the pure colors of the virtues, blended with one another by a kind of artistic mixing, in order to imitate the beauty. Then we become an image of the image, having taken the impression of the archetypal beauty through imitation as active as we can make it, as Paul did when he became an imitator of Christ through a life of virtue. If we must also set out in detail the things by which the image is imitated, one color is humility: "Learn from me," he says, "for I am gentle and humble in heart." Another color is long-suffering. How did it appear in the image of the invisible God? Swords and clubs, bonds and scourges, cheeks struck, a face spat upon, a back given over to blows, an impious tribunal, a harsh sentence, soldiers reveling in that grim sentence with mockery, taunts and blows from a reed, nails, gall, vinegar, and every most dreadful thing, all brought upon him without cause, or rather given in return for his many kinds of kindness. What, then, was his retaliation against those who did these things? "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing." Could he not have brought the heaven crashing down on them from above, or made the insolent vanish into a chasm in the earth, or cast the sea out beyond its bounds and sunk the land beneath the deep, or hurled on them the rain of fire that fell on Sodom, or done some other grim thing by his command? But he bore these things with gentleness and long-suffering, and by his own example he lays down long-suffering as a law for your life. In the same way all the other virtues can be seen in the archetypal image of God. Whoever looks at it and adorns his own form clearly after it becomes himself an image of the invisible God, painted by endurance. But whoever has learned that Christ is the head

of the Church should consider this before all else: every head is of the same nature and the same essence as the body beneath it, and there is a single natural union of the individual members with the whole, which through one common breath produces a fellow-feeling between the whole and its parts. So if anything is outside the body, it is certainly alien to the head as well. The word teaches us, then, that whatever the head is by nature, the individual members must also become, so that they may be akin to the head. And we are the members who make up the body of Christ. If, then, someone takes a member of Christ and makes it a member of a prostitute, he has thrust in licentious frenzy like a sword and has certainly cut that member off from the head by this evil passion. The other instruments of vice likewise become swords. By them the members are severed from the body to which they naturally belong and are separated from the head entirely, wherever the passions make their cut. So that the whole body may remain in its natural state, the individual members must also be akin to the head, joined, as it were, to the pure head in the principle of their being. If we conceive of the head as incorruption, the members too must certainly subsist in incorruption. The same holds for the other qualities by which the head is understood: it follows that they are seen in the members too, such as peace, sanctification, truth and all things of that kind. For through the Son these and similar things are displayed in the members, and they show that the members are naturally one with the head. So the Apostle says: he is the head, and from him the whole body, fitted and held together by every joint, according to the working in the measure of each individual part, brings about the body's growth. We should also learn this from the name "head." In living creatures, the impulse that starts the body's activities comes from the head, since every particular is directed by the eye and the hearing, both the movement of the feet and the work of the hands. It is impossible for any task in hand to be done properly if the eye is not watching over what is being done or the hearing is not receiving guidance. In the same way we, who are the body, must move in step with the true head in every impulse and activity, wherever he who formed the eye and planted the ear leads us. Since, then, the head looks to the things above, the members fitted to the head must certainly follow its guidance and incline toward the things above. When we hear that he is the firstborn of creation, the firstborn from the dead and the firstborn among many brothers, let us first dismiss the heretical notions, since these words give no support to their wicked invention of doctrines. After that, let us also consider what these words contribute to our moral life. For since the Only-begotten God, the [?] of the universe

[?] that the same one is called by both names, only-begotten and firstborn. Yet Scripture has said of the Word who was in the beginning that the Only-begotten God is the firstborn of all creation. It is fitting, then, to assign each of these names to the mystery of the truth and to distinguish them piously. The pre-eternal Word is Only-begotten, while the Word, having become flesh, became the firstborn of the creation that came about afterward in Christ. Whatever we understand when we learn that he is firstborn from the dead and firstborn among many brothers, we shall understand in the same way of the firstborn of creation. He becomes firstborn from the dead, then, by becoming the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, so as to open the way for the resurrection of the flesh. He was going to make us sons of day and sons of light through birth from above by water and Spirit, us who were formerly children of wrath by nature. So he himself leads the way in this birth in the stream of the Jordan, drawing down the grace of the Spirit upon the firstfruits of our nature. Thus all who are born into life through spiritual rebirth are called brothers of the one who was born first through water and Spirit. In the same way, when we understand him as firstborn of the creation that came about in Christ, we do not stray from pious belief. For since the old creation passed away, rendered useless by sin, a new creation of life necessarily took the place of what had vanished, and it is constituted through rebirth and resurrection from the dead. The Author of life led the way into it, and so he becomes and is called the firstborn of life. As for how one should deal with opponents, the more diligent will easily find in the little that has been said enough help in the defense of the truth. We shall now briefly go through how these words may be seen to contribute to the life of virtue. Reuben was the firstborn of those brought forth by birth after him. The features that appeared in those born after him resembled those of the firstborn and testified to their kinship with him, so that their brother-

hood was not in doubt, since their likeness of appearance bore witness to it. If, then, we too have become brothers of the Lord through a like rebirth by water and spirit, the Lord who for our sake became firstborn among many brothers, it would follow that we should show our kinship with him by the features of our life, as the firstborn of creation is formed in our life. What feature of his form have we learned from Scripture? The one we have often mentioned: "He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth." So if we are to be called brothers of the one who led the way in our birth, the sinlessness of our life will confirm our kinship with him, and no stain will separate us from union with purity. Moreover, the firstborn is righteousness and sanctification, love and redemption, and the like. So if our life too is marked by such things, we shall show clear signs of our noble birth, and anyone who sees these things in our life will bear witness that we are brothers of Christ. For he is the one who opened the door of resurrection for us, and for this reason he became the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. That we shall all rise in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, he showed by what he did both in his own case and in the case of others held by death. Yet not all who rise from the dust of the earth will meet an equal condition in the life to come. "We shall go forth," it says, "those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment." So if anyone's life is heading toward that fearful condemnation, then even if he happens to be numbered among the brothers of the Lord through birth from above, he gives the lie to that name, denying his kinship with the firstborn by the form of vice he bears. The mediator between God and men, who through himself joins humanity to God, joins only what is worthy of union with God. He made his own humanity his own by the power of the Godhead. That humanity was part of our common nature, yet it was not subject to the passions of nature that incite to sin ("For he committed no sin," it says, "nor was deceit found in his mouth"). In the same way he will bring each one of us into union with the Godhead, provided we bring with us nothing unworthy of union with the Divine. If someone is truly a temple of God and holds within himself no idol or image of vice, the mediator will take him into participation in the Godhead, since he has become pure enough to receive his purity. For wisdom will not enter a soul that devises evil, as the word says, and the pure in heart sees nothing in himself but God. Joined to God through incorruption, he has received within himself the whole good kingdom. What is said would become still clearer if the Lord's words, which he spoke to the apostles through Mary, [?]

…we may also grasp the plain sense of what was said. "I am going," he says, "to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God." For it is the mediator between the Father and those who had been disowned who says this, he who through himself reconciled the enemies of God to the true and only Godhead. According to the prophetic word, human beings were estranged through sin from the life-giving womb and went astray from the belly in which they were formed, speaking falsehood instead of truth. For this reason he took up the firstfruits of our common nature, in both soul and body, and made it holy, keeping it in himself unmixed with all evil and closed to it. He did this so that, having offered it up through incorruptibility to the Father of incorruptibility, he might draw along with it everything that is akin to it by nature and of the same race, and receive the disowned into adoption and the enemies of God into a share in his Godhead. So, just as the firstfruits of the lump were made the true Father and God's own through purity and freedom from passion, we too, the lump, will be joined to the Father of incorruptibility by the same ways, by imitating as far as we can the mediator's freedom from passion and his unchangeableness. In this way we will become a crown of precious stones for the Only-begotten God, having become honor and glory through our life. For Paul says, "You made him a little lower than the angels" because of the suffering of death. Those who had earlier been changed into the nature of thorns through sin he made into a crown for himself through the dispensation of his death, transforming the thorn by his suffering into honor and glory. So the danger is not small. Once he who takes away the sin of the world has taken the crown of thorns on his head in order to make the crown woven of honor and glory, someone may be found who through his wicked life is [?] a thorn, and is then threaded into the midst of the Lord's crown through his share in the body. To such a person the just voice will say: "How did you get in here without a wedding garment?" How did you, a thorn, become entwined with those fitted into my crown through honor and glory? "What agreement has Christ with Belial? What share has a believer with unbelievers? What does light have in common with darkness?" So that our life may never call down such words against us, we must take care to clear every thorny deed, word and thought out of the whole course of our life. Then, having become honor and glory through a pure way of life free from passion, we may crown the head of all through ourselves, becoming for him a kind of treasure and [?] possession. For the Lord of glory does not allow himself to be, or to be called, the Lord of anything dishonorable. So the person who is a stranger to all shame and vileness, in both the hidden and the visible self, makes his master the one who both is and is called Lord of glory, not of dishonor. He is also called "the beginning." The beginning of anything is not foreign to what comes after it. For if someone defines the beginning as life,

what comes after the beginning will certainly be understood as life too. And if the beginning is light, what comes after the beginning will also be understood as light. What, then, do we gain by believing that he is the beginning? We gain this: we become what we have believed our beginning to be. For light is not called the beginning of darkness, and when life is set as the beginning, we do not take death to be the continuation of life. Unless someone shares the nature of what leads him, joined to the beginning through freedom from passion and through virtue, the beginning of all things would not become his beginning. The beginning of a dark life is the world-ruler of darkness, and the beginning of death-bringing sin is the one who has the power of death. So a person who is placed under the rule of darkness by a wicked life cannot say that the beginning of all good is his own beginning. The same thought applies, for those who take the divine words for their own good, to the fact that he is also named King of righteousness and of peace. Following the teaching of the prayer, a person prays that the kingdom of God may come upon him. Having learned that the true King is King of righteousness and peace, he will certainly achieve righteousness and peace in his own life, so that the King of righteousness and peace whom he prays for may reign over him. Every virtue, then, is understood as the King's army, for I think that by righteousness and peace we must understand all the virtues. Suppose someone deserts from the army of God and enlists himself in the ranks of the foreigners, becoming a soldier of the inventor of evil, stripping off the breastplate of righteousness and the whole armor of peace. How will he be ranked under the King of peace, when he has thrown away the shield of truth? Clearly the emblem on his armor will show who reigns over him. Instead of the image painted on his weapons, he shows his leader in the character of his life. How blessed is the one who is placed under the divine command, enrolled in the companies of those numbered by myriads, and armed against evil with the virtues, which bear the image of the King who put them on! But why carry the discussion further, setting out in the order of our inquiry all the terms by which the name of Christ is interpreted? They can guide us toward the life of virtue, since each name, by its own particular meaning, surely contributes something to the perfecting of our life. Still, I think it is well to sum up what we have already mentioned, to give us some guidance toward the aim we set for this discussion at the start, when we asked how a person might achieve perfection in himself. I think that if someone always keeps in mind that he shares in the name we worship, being called a Christian according to the teaching of the apostles, he will necessarily also display in himself the power of the other names by which Christ is understood, coming through his life to share in each title.

I mean something like this. Three things mark the Christian's life: action, word and thought. Thought is the beginning of every word. The word comes second, after thinking, and through the voice it reveals the thought imprinted on the soul. Action holds third place, after mind and word, and puts what was thought into effect. So when any one of these leads us onward in our life, it is well to examine carefully, in every word, deed and thought, these divine concepts by which the Lord is understood and named. Then our deed, word or thought will not stray outside the power of those lofty names. Paul says that everything that is not of faith is sin. In the same way, anyone who follows the argument can plainly declare that everything which does not look to Christ, whether word, deed or thought, surely looks to the opposite. One who has come to be outside light or life cannot help being in darkness or in death. If, then, whatever is done, said and thought not in accordance with Christ belongs with what is opposed to the good, it should be clear to everyone from this that the person who has gone outside Christ abandons him through what he thinks, does or says. So the divine voice of the prophet speaks the truth when it says, "I counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors." The person who denied Christ in the persecutions is a transgressor of the name we worship. In the same way, suppose someone denies truth or righteousness, or holiness and incorruptibility, or casts out of his life anything else that counts as virtue when the passions get the upper hand. The prophecy calls him a transgressor, because through each of these he transgresses in his life against the one who is these things. What, then, must a person do who has been counted worthy of the great name of Christ? What else, but constantly test his thoughts, words and deeds within himself, to see whether each of them looks toward Christ or has become estranged from Christ? It is very easy to tell these things apart. Whatever is done, thought or said through some passion has no harmony with Christ but bears the stamp of the adversary. He smears the passions like mud on the pearl of the soul and spoils the brilliance of the precious stone. But whatever is pure of every passionate disposition looks to the author of freedom from passion, who is Christ. Whoever draws his thoughts from him, as from a pure and unobstructed spring, will show the same likeness to the original that water has to water: the water bubbling up at the spring and the water that has come from there into the jar. For the purity seen in Christ and the purity seen in the one who shares in him are one in nature. But he is the spring, while the one who shares in him draws from it and carries the beauty of his thoughts over into his life. In this way the hidden self is in harmony with the visible self, as the

good order of a person's life matches the movements of the heart that follow Christ. In my judgment, then, this is perfection in the Christian life: to share, in soul, in speech and in the pursuits of life, in all the names that are signified by the name of Christ. Then, according to Paul's blessing, a person keeps complete holiness in himself, in the whole of body, soul and spirit, guarded at all times from any mixture with evil. But someone may say that this is hard to achieve. Only the Lord of creation is unchangeable, while human nature is changeable and prone to alteration. How, then, can steadfastness and constancy in the good be achieved in a changeable nature? To such an argument we reply that no one is crowned who has not competed according to the rules, and there can be no lawful contest without an opponent. If there were no adversary, there would be no crown either, for victory does not exist by itself without something that is defeated. Let us therefore contend against this very changeability of our nature, grappling with it in our thoughts as with an opponent. We become victors not by throwing it down but by not allowing it to fall. For human beings do not use change only for evil. If by nature we tended only toward the opposite of the good, it would be impossible for us ever to come to be in the good. As it is, the finest work of change is growth in good things, as alteration for the better keeps transforming the one who is well altered into something more divine. So the argument has shown that what seems frightening, I mean that our nature is changeable, is like a wing for flight toward greater things. It would be a loss to us if we could not undergo alteration for the better. Let no one be grieved, then, when he sees in his nature a capacity for change. Let him always be altered for the better and transformed from glory to glory. Let him change in this way, always becoming better through daily growth, always being perfected, and never reaching the limit of perfection. For this is truly perfection: never to stop growing toward the better, and never to confine perfection within any limit.
